questions.question: On most coasts, the sea creeps up the beach and slides back down it again, day after day, and fishermen and swimmers plan around these tides. What mainly causes the tides?
questions.answer: The pull of the Moon's gravity
choices: The pull of the Moon's gravity
The push of the wind on the sea
The warmth of the Sun on the sea
The pull of Earth's magnetism
questions.context: The Moon's gravity tugs on Earth's oceans and heaps the water up, and as Earth turns, each coast moves into the high water and out of it again; the Sun's gravity adds a smaller share. Strong winds can pile water against a shore in a storm, but they do not make the steady rise and fall of the tides.
questions.grade_note: That the Moon's gravity causes the tides is the heart of the 6th-grade tides standard, and wind is the cause students most often guess.

questions.question: The Moon's gravity heaps the ocean up into a broad mound on the side of Earth that faces the Moon. At the same moment, what is the ocean doing on the side of Earth that faces away from the Moon?
choices: Rising into high water
Sinking into extra-low water
Lying level, neither high nor low
Draining away toward the Moon's side
questions.context: The Moon pulls hardest on the near side of Earth and most weakly on the far side, so as Earth is pulled toward the Moon, the far-side water is left behind in a second bulge. Earth spins through both bulges, so most coasts get two high tides about every day, with the low tides in the low places between them.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade lessons draw two tidal bulges, one facing the Moon and one opposite, to explain two high tides a day; a single bulge facing the Moon is the usual mistake.

questions.question: A girl pushes a stick into the sand at the water's edge just at high tide. The sea slides away down the beach and then creeps back up to her stick. On most coasts, about how long after one high tide does the next high tide come?
choices: About 12 hours and 25 minutes
About 6 hours and 12 minutes
About 24 hours and 50 minutes
About 3 hours and 6 minutes
questions.context: Most coasts get two high tides and two low tides every 24 hours and 50 minutes, so the high tides come about 12 hours and 25 minutes apart. Low tide falls about halfway between, some six hours after each high.
questions.grade_note: Two high and two low tides a day, a little over 12 hours apart, is the basic tide pattern 6th graders learn and read from tide tables.

questions.question: A fisherman notices that high tide at his harbour comes about 50 minutes later each day than it did the day before. Why do the tides keep slipping later?
questions.answer: The Moon moves on along its path around Earth
choices: The Moon moves on along its path around Earth
Earth moves on along its path around the Sun
The wind holds the tide back a little more each day
The sea rises a little more slowly each day
questions.context: The Moon travels around Earth in the same direction that Earth spins, so by the time Earth has made one full turn, the Moon has moved on, and Earth needs about 50 minutes more to bring the harbour back under the Moon. Earth's trip around the Sun sets the length of the year, not the daily timing of the tides. Wind can push the sea about in a storm, but it changes from day to day and cannot keep so steady a timetable.
questions.grade_note: 6th graders see in tide tables that each tide comes about 50 minutes later each day, and the Moon's motion along its orbit is the simple reason taught.

questions.question: The Sun has about 27 million times as much mass as the Moon. Yet the tides that the Sun raises on Earth's oceans are only about half as big as the Moon's. Why does the Sun raise smaller tides?
questions.answer: It is much farther away from Earth
choices: It is much farther away from Earth
It is made of hot gas, not solid rock
It pulls on the sea only in the daytime
Its pull is shared out among all the planets
questions.context: The Sun is nearly 400 times farther from Earth than the Moon. A tide comes from how much harder a body pulls on Earth's near side than on its far side, and that difference fades very fast with distance, even faster than the pull itself. Gravity depends on mass and distance, not on what a body is made of, and the Sun's pull works on all of Earth, night and day, however many planets it also holds.
questions.grade_note: The 6th-grade tides standard names the Sun's pull as well as the Moon's, and the Sun's far greater distance is the simple reason taught for its smaller effect.

questions.question: A harbour master keeps a daily record of the tides. On some days the Sun, the Moon and Earth lie in one straight line in space. What does his record show for the tides around those days?
questions.answer: Higher high tides and lower low tides
choices: Higher high tides and lower low tides
Higher high tides, but the same low tides
Lower high tides and higher low tides
Twice as many high and low tides
questions.context: With the Sun, the Moon and Earth in line, the Sun's tide adds to the Moon's. The bulges grow taller, and the extra water heaped into them is drawn from the low places between, so the high tides rise higher and the low tides fall lower. These tides, with the biggest range between high and low, are called spring tides.
questions.grade_note: 6th graders learn that when the Sun, the Moon and Earth line up, the two pulls add and give spring tides, with the greatest range between high and low tide.

questions.question: At the first and third quarter moons, the Sun and the Moon sit at a right angle to each other as seen from Earth. The tides then rise and fall less than at any other time of the month. What are these tides called?
choices: Neap tides
Spring tides
Ebb tides
Slack tides
questions.context: Neap tides come at the quarter moons, when the Moon looks half lit. The Sun's pull then works across the Moon's and partly cancels it, so the range between high and low tide is the smallest. An ebb tide is simply a falling tide, and slack water is the brief still pause when the tide turns.
questions.grade_note: Neap tides at the quarter moons, with the smallest tidal range, are named beside spring tides in the 6th-grade tides standard.

questions.question: Sailors and fishermen check their tide tables for spring tides, which come when the Sun, the Moon and Earth line up. How often do spring tides come?
questions.answer: Twice a month, all year round
choices: Twice a month, all year round
Twice a month, in spring only
Once a year, in the springtime
Once a month, all year round
questions.context: Spring tides come around every new moon and every full moon, the two times in each month when the Sun, the Moon and Earth line up, so they come about twice a month in every season of the year. The name has nothing to do with spring: it comes from the water springing up.
questions.grade_note: 6th-grade lessons stress that spring tides come about twice a month all year, because students link the name to the season.

The key is now 'Rising into high water', which also drops 'up into', a phrase it shared with the stem ('heaps the ocean up into') and no lure did; 'Sinking down into' becomes 'Sinking into' to stay parallel. Context: the Sun-orbit sentence becomes the wind's, and 'not the tides' becomes 'not the daily timing of the tides' (fact-check's optional wording). Stem and key unchanged.

872deb5a0c.why: Judge (medium): two lures were weak ('blocked by Earth's air', 'its heat keeps the sea from rising'). They are replaced by the judge's live naive ideas, 'It pulls on the sea only in the daytime' (false: the Sun's pull acts on all of Earth and its tide runs on a 12-hour cycle, F23, new) and 'Its pull is shared out among all the planets' (false: the pull between two bodies depends only on their masses and distance, F12). 'Made of hot gas' kept. Context: '390 times' is now 'nearly 400 times', to agree with moon-phases-and-eclipses (judge's unit note), and it now says why the two new lures are wrong. Stem and key unchanged.

754ec2c299.why: Judge (low, fixed because it removes a leak): the stem stated the key of 20e142e1f0 ('the highest high tides and the lowest low tides'). Spring tides are now defined by the line-up instead (the judge's wording), which also makes the question the grade's simple why. Context: 'at every new moon' is now 'around every new moon' (fact-check's optional wording: the biggest tides often lag by a day). Key and choices unchanged.

dropped.question: Suppose the Moon vanished one night, while Earth went on spinning and travelling around the Sun just as before. What would happen to the tides in Earth's oceans?
dropped.why: Judge (medium): its fact, that the Sun raises tides of its own about half the Moon's, is stated in the stem of 872deb5a0c and assumed by 20e142e1f0 and 4078fe05a9, so a player gets it free; two of its lures drew no one. The judge's re-key on the Moon's nearest point (F19) was weighed and not used: with 872deb5a0c keying distance, and the common sense that a nearer Moon pulls harder, its answer would be free as well.
